Stocks Fell 6 Days in a Row. Is a Crash Coming?

2026-11-20

About this video

The S&P 500 fell 6 days in a row and closed at 7,175.83 on Nov 19, 2026: 8.2% below its Oct 6 record of 7,818.93. The Nasdaq is 13.5% below its record (a correction) and the Dow closed at 49,097.06, below 50,000 for the first time since June. Why: the 10-year Treasury yield is 5.07%, inflation is 4.1%, and the Fed raised rates in September. Then the history: since 1950 the S&P 500 fell 8% or more from a record 37 times, and 11 of those became bear markets. The S&P 500 just fell 6 days in a row. It's now 8.2 percent below its record. The Dow is 9.7 percent down, and the Nasdaq is down 13.5 percent, which puts it in what Wall Street calls a correction. So is a crash coming? Here's the short answer from history. Since 1950, the S&P 500 has fallen 8 percent or more from a record 37 times. Only 11 of those turned into a bear market. Most drops this size ended without a crash. But most isn't all. In this video: what happened this week, why stocks are falling, what history says about drops like this, and what it means for your money. If that's useful, subscribe: we break down money news like this every day. Let's start with this week. On November 11, the S&P 500 closed at 7,619. Then it fell. And fell again. 6 trading days, 6 losses. Over those 6 days, the index dropped 5.8 percent. Today alone, it fell 2.0 percent, and the Dow lost about 1,101 points. To put that in dollars: if you had 10,000 dollars in an S&P 500 index fund on November 11, it was worth about 9,418 dollars at today's close. Quick refresher. The S&P 500 tracks 500 of the biggest U.S. companies. The Dow tracks just 30 big, well-known ones. And the Nasdaq Composite holds thousands of stocks, with a lot of tech. If you have a 401(k) or an index fund, there's a good chance you own a slice of these companies. So when the indexes fall, your balance usually falls with them. Here's how far each of the big three indexes is below its record high. Wall Street has names for these drops. Down 10 percent from a record is called a correction. Down 20 percent is a bear market. The Nasdaq, packed with tech stocks, is down 13.5 percent from its October 6 record. That's a correction. The S&P 500 isn't there yet. And the Dow, which first closed above 50,000 in February, fell back below it today, for the first time since June. For the S&P 500 to officially enter a correction, it would have to close below about 7,037. Today it closed at 7,176. In dollars: 10,000 dollars put into an S&P 500 fund at the October 6 record is worth about 9,178 dollars today. But 10,000 dollars put in ten years ago, in November 2016, is worth about 32,888 dollars today, even after this drop. Both numbers count prices only, not dividends. Same index, very different feelings. What matters most is how long you hold, not the week you're in. So why are stocks falling? Reason one: interest rates. The 10-year Treasury yield, what the U.S. government pays to borrow for ten years, is at 5.07 percent. A year ago, it was 4.12 percent. Think about it from an investor's side. A government bond now pays over 5 percent a year, with almost no risk. A stock promises nothing. So when safe bonds pay this much, stocks have to compete, and investors pay less for them. Reason two: inflation. Prices rose 4.1 percent in the year to October, according to the Consumer Price Index. To fight it, the Federal Reserve raised its interest rate on September 17, its first hike since 2023, back to 3.75 to 4.00 percent. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive for companies and families. That can slow spending and profits, and stock prices follow profits. It's already hitting wallets. The average 30-year mortgage rate is 7.28 percent, up from 6.24 a year ago, according to Freddie Mac. And the prime rate, the base for most credit card rates, is 7 percent. Reason three: the stocks that rose the most are falling the most. Look at the tech-heavy Nasdaq against the Dow this year. The Nasdaq ran up faster, and since its October record it has fallen 13.5 percent. When investors take profits, the biggest winners usually drop first, and fastest. At its peak this year, the Nasdaq was up 18.7 percent. Now it's up just 2.7 percent for 2026. The Dow was up as much as 13.1 percent, and now it's up 2.2. Now the big question. Does a drop like this turn into a crash? We looked at every S&P 500 decline since 1950. 37 times, the index fell 8 percent or more from a record. 26 of those kept going to 10 percent or more. And 11 became bear markets, with drops of 20 percent or more. So roughly 7 out of 10 drops that reached 8 percent never became bear markets. But about 3 in 10 did, so nobody can promise this one stops here. Let's look at the two most recent big drops. In 2020, when the pandemic hit, the S&P 500 fell 34 percent in about a month, to a low on March 23. It was back at a record by August 18, and the year ended 16 percent higher. 2022 was different. Inflation and rate hikes pushed the index down 25 percent by October. It didn't reach a new record until January 2024, more than a year later. For a typical correction, between 10 and 20 percent, the S&P 500 took about 7 months to get from its old record back to a new one. Some drops heal fast. Some take years. What about losing streaks? Since 1950, the S&P 500 has had 116 six-day losing streaks. The last one before this week was in April 2024. A year after those streaks, stocks were higher 91 times out of 116. The median gain over that year was about 13 percent, not counting dividends. But 25 times, stocks were still lower a year later. Streaks tell you how people feel. They don't predict the future. That April 2024 streak ended with the S&P 500 near 4,967. A year later, it was about 8 percent higher. Here's something most people don't know. Big drops happen almost every year, even in good years. The red bars show each year's worst drop. The green bars show where the year ended. Since 1950, the typical year had a drop of about 10 percent along the way. And yet, 55 of the last 75 full years ended higher. One more pattern. Of the 10 best days for the S&P 500 since 1950, 8 came within two weeks of one of the 20 worst days. The best day of all, a 11.6 percent gain, came in October 2008, right in the middle of the financial crisis. That's why selling in a panic can be costly: the rebound often comes when things look worst. So what decides where stocks go from here? Here are four things to watch. First, the 10-year Treasury yield. If it keeps climbing past 5 percent, stocks face more pressure. If it falls, they get relief. Second, the next inflation reports. Third, the Federal Reserve's meeting in December, where it decides whether to raise rates again. And fourth, jobs and company profits: as long as people are working and companies are earning, a drop is less likely to turn into a recession. So what does this mean for you? Here's what most financial educators point to. Money you'll need in the next few years usually doesn't belong in stocks, because a drop like this can come at the wrong moment. For long-term money, time has mattered more than timing. Spreading money across many investments limits the damage from any one of them. And an emergency fund means you never have to sell at the bottom. And if you invest every month, through a 401(k) for example, lower prices mean each contribution buys more shares. Let's recap. The S&P 500 fell 6 days in a row and is 8 percent below its record. The Nasdaq is in a correction. Bonds pay 5.1 percent, inflation is 4.1 percent, and the Fed is raising rates.
